subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the carbon cycle, by which two processes is carbon returned to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide?
questions.explain: Respiration by living organisms and combustion of fuels both release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere.

questions.q: Antigenic variation makes some pathogens (e.g. influenza virus) hard to combat because:
options: They change their surface antigens, so memory cells from previous infections no longer recognise them
They destroy all the host's T-cells
They cannot be engulfed by phagocytes
They reproduce too slowly for memory cells to form
questions.explain: Frequent changes to surface antigens mean existing memory cells are no longer complementary, so a new primary response is needed each time.

questions.q: Forty animals are marked and released; later 50 are captured, of which 10 are marked. What is the estimated population size?
questions.explain: N = (40 x 50) / 10 = 200 individuals.

questions.q: In the Hardy-Weinberg equations, q squared represents the frequency of:
questions.explain: q squared is the frequency of the homozygous recessive genotype, since q is the recessive allele frequency.

questions.q: Which process in the nitrogen cycle returns nitrogen gas to the atmosphere, reducing soil fertility?
questions.explain: Denitrifying bacteria in anaerobic soils convert nitrate back to nitrogen gas, lowering soil nitrogen.

questions.q: Which equation correctly expresses net primary productivity (NPP)?
questions.explain: NPP is the energy left for growth after the producers' respiratory losses are subtracted from GPP.

questions.q: Sympatric speciation in plants can arise rapidly through polyploidy because polyploid offspring:
options: Cannot interbreed with the diploid parent population, creating instant reproductive isolation
questions.explain: Polyploids cannot produce fertile offspring with diploid parents, instantly isolating them reproductively.

questions.q: Receiving an injection of antibodies (e.g. anti-tetanus serum) provides:
questions.explain: Ready-made antibodies are introduced artificially without the body making its own, giving immediate but short-lived (passive) protection.

questions.q: In a pyramid of energy, why is each successive trophic level smaller, and why is a pyramid of energy never inverted?
options: Energy increases up the food chain
Energy is lost at each transfer, so less is always available to the next level
Energy is created at each level
questions.explain: Because energy is lost as heat and in unconsumed material at every transfer, each level always has less energy than the one below.

questions.q: Monoclonal antibodies are described as 'monoclonal' because they are:
options: A mixture of antibodies against several antigens
Made only inside the human body
Identical antibodies produced from a single clone of cells, all specific to one antigen
questions.explain: They are derived from one B-cell clone, so every antibody is identical and binds the same specific antigen.

questions.q: Hybrid sterility, such as the infertile mule from a horse and donkey, is an example of a:
questions.explain: The hybrid forms but is sterile, so isolation acts after the zygote forms, making it postzygotic.

questions.q: Directional selection is characterised by:
options: The population mean shifting towards one extreme phenotype
Both extremes being favoured over the mean
questions.explain: Directional selection favours one extreme, shifting the population mean in that direction over time.

questions.q: In the biological species concept, two organisms belong to the same species if they can:
questions.explain: The biological species concept defines a species as a group able to interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

questions.q: Allopatric speciation occurs when populations are reproductively isolated by:
options: A behavioural difference within the same area
A change in mating season only
A geographical barrier such as a mountain or river
questions.explain: In allopatric speciation a physical/geographical barrier separates populations, allowing them to diverge.

questions.q: Which describes a density-independent factor affecting a population?
options: Disease spread in a crowded population
A severe frost killing organisms regardless of population size
questions.explain: A frost affects the same proportion of individuals whatever the density, so it is density-independent.

questions.q: The Hardy-Weinberg principle predicts that allele and genotype frequencies remain constant only if:
options: There is no mutation, no selection, no migration, random mating and a large population
The population is small with frequent migration
questions.explain: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium assumes a large population with no mutation, selection or migration and random mating.

questions.q: For herd immunity to interrupt transmission of a pathogen, the proportion of the population that must be immune depends mainly on:
options: The age of the youngest individual
How easily the pathogen spreads from person to person
The colour of the vaccine vial
questions.explain: More infectious pathogens require a higher proportion of immune individuals to break chains of transmission and protect the susceptible.

questions.q: Modern classification places organisms into three domains. These are:
questions.explain: The three-domain system divides life into Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya based largely on rRNA sequence differences.

questions.q: Herd immunity protects unvaccinated individuals because:
options: The pathogen mutates to become harmless
Antibodies are passed between people on contact
Vaccines spread immunity through the air
A high proportion of immune people reduces the chance of an unvaccinated person meeting an infected person
questions.explain: When enough of the population is immune, transmission is interrupted, so susceptible individuals are unlikely to encounter the pathogen.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections such as HIV?
options: Viruses are too large to be affected
Viruses lack the metabolic processes and structures (e.g. cell walls, ribosomes) that antibiotics target
questions.explain: Antibiotics target bacterial structures and processes; viruses use host-cell machinery and lack these targets, so antibiotics do not affect them.

questions.q: How does ploughing and draining waterlogged soil tend to affect the nitrogen available to crops?
options: It converts nitrate to nitrogen gas
It improves aeration, favouring nitrifying bacteria and reducing denitrification
questions.explain: Better aeration favours aerobic nitrifying bacteria and limits anaerobic denitrifiers, so more nitrate remains for plants.

questions.q: HIV cannot replicate without a host cell because it:
options: Is too small to contain genetic material
Lacks the enzymes and ribosomes needed for protein synthesis and energy release
questions.explain: As a virus, HIV has no metabolic machinery of its own and must use the host cell's enzymes and ribosomes to replicate.

questions.q: An antibody is a glycoprotein with a quaternary structure made up of:
options: Two heavy and two light polypeptide chains held by disulfide bonds
One heavy and three light chains
questions.explain: Each antibody consists of two identical heavy and two identical light chains linked by disulfide bridges, forming a Y-shaped molecule.

questions.q: A condition occurs in 1 in 10 000 people and is caused by a homozygous recessive genotype. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the recessive allele frequency (q) is:
questions.explain: q squared = 1/10 000 = 0.0001, so q = the square root of 0.0001 = 0.01.

questions.q: The founder effect occurs when:
options: A large population is split equally by a barrier
A small group establishes a new population carrying only a subset of the original gene pool
questions.explain: A few founding individuals carry only part of the parent population's genetic variation, skewing allele frequencies in the new population.

questions.q: What is the role of saprobiotic (decomposer) bacteria and fungi in ammonification?
options: They release nitrogen gas from nitrate
They convert nitrogen-containing compounds in dead matter into ammonium ions
questions.explain: Decomposers break down proteins and other nitrogen compounds in dead organisms, releasing ammonium ions.

questions.q: A low index of diversity in a habitat suggests an ecosystem that is:
options: Highly stable and resistant to change
Dominated by few species and more vulnerable to environmental change
questions.explain: Low diversity indicates few species or uneven abundance, making the ecosystem less stable and more vulnerable.

questions.q: The maximum population size an environment can support sustainably is known as the:
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is the maximum population an ecosystem's resources can support over a long period.

questions.q: After engulfing a pathogen, a macrophage often becomes an antigen-presenting cell. This means it:
options: Stores the antigens permanently inside vesicles
Destroys all lymphocytes that bind to it
Displays the pathogen's antigens on its surface to activate lymphocytes
questions.explain: By presenting antigens on its surface, the macrophage activates specific T-helper cells, linking innate and adaptive immunity.

questions.q: In the nitrogen cycle, which process converts atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonia or ammonium ions?
questions.explain: Nitrogen fixation, carried out by bacteria such as Rhizobium and Azotobacter, converts N2 into ammonia.
